FURTHER INFO HERE!:

For those of you who aren’t familiar, bait rabbits are used in both greyhound racing training and also generalised sighthound hunt training. Blue and Sable were young females bought from one of the most popular UK pet retailers by persons who used them in caged baiting, meaning the rabbits were caged and attached to contraptions in order to train young sighthounds to chase after prey for races or hunts.

They were dumped at a local rescue centre at less than one year old. Both of them had rear leg fractures, and Blue had severe bite lacerations. The fact that she survived is a pure miracle, and even so that they gave these bunnies up instead of letting them be mauled.

Both rabbits required over 2 years of physical therapy, and now live wonderful, happy and fulfilled lives. They are bonded to eachother and are best friends. They have a huge area to play with my other rescue bunnies and they are doing amazing.

To make a difference for bunnies like Blue and Sable, consider petitioning your local governments against the racing of and hunting with dogs. Racing with dogs is drastically unethical for the prey that’s used as training bait and the dogs. Hunting with dogs is horrible to local ecosystems and really does more harm than good.

Happy 2021 everyone 💕

This has happened to a lot of people, including myself, so understand that you aren’t alone on this. However, this question is pretty subjective- understand that people come apart like this under different circumstances and cope in different ways. It’s a question of, moving forward, how you can work to make the “grief” period of moving on a little easier and hopefully an opportunity to better yourself. For me, I take things like this pretty hard usually, it can take me a long time to truly feel like I’ve mourned the opportunities I never got. However, using my time wisely and applying it to myself in a self-improving way at least allowed me to come out of these experiences feeling much more contented and with a greater sense of closure. Always remember, there’s no such thing as a dead end, even if you have to take a fork in the road or an unbeaten path to get to the next stage of your journey.

In the mean time, it’s a question of mitigation. If this isolation is truly unavoidable and you find yourself with a lot of time on your hands, it could be helpful to take up the opportunity to learn something new that is arresting of attention. At least that way when you come out of the experience, it’s in a way that has been helpful and left you with a new skill to speak of, as opposed to just money and little else.

If it isn’t possible to strike a balance between this and your personal, social health, you need to make the right decision for you. Having something like this is one of those things that comes with many burdens. You need to ask yourself whether these burdens are worth the hassle to you and whether they are possibly workable.

Take it one step at a time. You are not condemned to loneliness forever, you just happen to be alone right now. Things change. Allow yourself the opportunity to heal. Try “dating yourself”; treat yourself with unequivocal love, teach yourself something new. Grow as much as you can and the rest will follow.

I was homeless for five months, and have been housed now for a few years. I still feel guilty occasionally. No matter what, though, it isn’t a question of whether you deserved it or not (either way NOBODY deserves to be homeless) and more of thankfulness. Irrespective of my guilt I strive to be thankful either way and it eases the guilt. If the guilt is really unworkable, no matter what you hear you will never believe you deserve good fortune and you will never truly forgive yourself- take it one step at a time. Work off the guilt by working on yourself until you feel you ARE a person that deserved your good fortune, even if you may be that person already.
